claims.text: When to use it Blunt abdominal trauma (especially hypotensive); rapid bedside triage when CT is not feasible. Helps decide OR vs CT in unstable patients. Less reliable for penetrating trauma
claims.quote: Indications: blunt abdominal trauma (especially hypotensive); rapid bedside triage when CT not feasible. Helps decide OR vs CT in unstable patients. Less reliable for penetrating trauma.

claims.text: Probe: curvilinear or phased-array for the four standard FAST views; linear probe for the eFAST anterior chest views (pneumothorax)
claims.quote: Probe: curvilinear or phased-array for the four standard FAST views; linear probe for the eFAST anterior chest views (pneumothorax).

claims.text: Sequence (typical): 1. Pericardial (subxiphoid) → 2. RUQ (Morison's pouch) → 3. LUQ (perisplenic) → 4. Suprapubic. Add bilateral anterior chest views = eFAST
claims.quote: Sequence (typical): 1. Pericardial (subxiphoid) → 2. RUQ (Morison's pouch) → 3. LUQ (perisplenic) → 4. Suprapubic. Add bilateral anterior chest views = eFAST.

claims.text: How good is it Sensitivity ~80% / specificity > 90% for hemoperitoneum; minimum detectable free fluid ~200-250 mL. Trendelenburg may improve sensitivity in the RUQ
claims.quote: Performance: sensitivity ~80% / specificity >90% for hemoperitoneum; minimum detectable free fluid ~200-250 mL. Trendelenburg may improve sensitivity in RUQ.

claims.text: A negative FAST does NOT rule out injury. In stable patients with a concerning mechanism / exam, get CT. Serial FAST may detect evolving hemorrhage
claims.quote: Key limitation: a negative FAST does NOT rule out injury. In stable patients with concerning mechanism / exam, get CT. Serial FAST may detect evolving hemorrhage.

claims.text: Pneumothorax: US sensitivity ~88-90% (better than supine CXR ~50%), specificity ~99%. Hemothorax: US can detect as little as ~20 mL of pleural fluid
claims.quote: For pneumothorax: US sensitivity ~88-90% (better than supine CXR ~50%); specificity ~99%. For hemothorax: US can detect as little as ~20 mL of pleural fluid.
claims.locator: FAST & eFAST Exam, Indications, Probe, Sequence, Performance

claims.text: Pericardial view (subxiphoid; alternative parasternal) Probe: just inferior and right of the xiphoid, indicator to the patient's right, beam aimed toward the left shoulder; liver as the acoustic window. Alternative: parasternal long axis
claims.quote: Probe just inferior & right of xiphoid, indicator to patient's right, beam aimed toward left shoulder; use liver as acoustic window. Alternative: parasternal long axis.

claims.text: Look for: anechoic stripe in the pericardial sac → pericardial effusion. RV diastolic collapse + RA systolic collapse + plethoric IVC → tamponade physiology
claims.quote: Anechoic stripe in pericardial sac → pericardial effusion. RV diastolic collapse + RA systolic collapse + plethoric IVC → tamponade physiology.

claims.text: Pitfalls: tell pericardial from pleural fluid using the descending aorta (pericardial fluid is anterior to it on PSLA). An epicardial fat pad can mimic a small effusion — usually anterior only
claims.quote: Distinguish pericardial from pleural fluid using descending aorta as landmark (pericardial is anterior to descending aorta on PSLA). Epicardial fat pad can mimic small effusion - usually anterior only.

claims.text: RUQ view (Morison's pouch / hepatorenal) Probe: mid-axillary line, ~10th-11th intercostal space, indicator cephalad. See the liver tip, hepatorenal recess (Morison's pouch) and right hemidiaphragm/subphrenic space
claims.quote: Mid-axillary line, ~10th-11th intercostal space, indicator cephalad. Visualize liver tip, hepatorenal recess (Morison's pouch), and right hemidiaphragm/subphrenic space.

claims.text: Look for: most sensitive view for hemoperitoneum in a supine patient. Anechoic stripe between liver and kidney = free fluid. Also check above the diaphragm for hemothorax (anechoic above the bright diaphragm)
claims.quote: Most sensitive view for hemoperitoneum in supine patient. Anechoic stripe between liver & kidney = free fluid. Also assess above diaphragm for hemothorax (anechoic above bright diaphragm).

claims.text: Pitfalls: sweep the whole interface; small pockets are often at the hepatic tip or caudal to the liver. Perinephric fat may mimic free fluid (it is hypoechoic but follows the kidney contour)
claims.quote: Sweep through entire interface; small fluid pockets often at hepatic tip or caudal to liver. Perinephric fat may mimic free fluid (perirenal fat is hypoechoic but follows kidney contour).

claims.text: LUQ view (splenorenal / perisplenic) Probe: more posterior and cephalad than RUQ (“knuckles to the bed”), ~8th-10th intercostal space at the posterior axillary line, indicator cephalad; spleen as the window
claims.quote: More posterior & cephalad than RUQ - 'knuckles to the bed', ~8th-10th intercostal space at posterior axillary line, indicator cephalad. Spleen as window.

claims.text: Look for: free fluid often appears between spleen and diaphragm (subphrenic) first — look there before the splenorenal interface. Also check above the diaphragm for hemothorax
claims.quote: Free fluid often appears between spleen and diaphragm (subphrenic) first - look there before splenorenal interface. Also assess above diaphragm for hemothorax.

claims.text: Pitfalls: the spleen is smaller and more posterior than the liver — rib shadows often obscure it; reposition between rib spaces. Stomach gas is a confounder
claims.quote: Spleen is smaller and more posterior than liver - rib shadows commonly obscure view; reposition probe between rib spaces. Stomach gas is a confounder.

claims.text: Suprapubic view (pelvic / pouch of Douglas) Probe: just above the pubic symphysis in the midline; rock the probe down into the pelvis; scan transverse and longitudinal. Best with a full bladder (acoustic window)
claims.quote: Just superior to pubic symphysis in midline; rock probe down into pelvis. Scan both transverse & longitudinal. Best with full bladder (acoustic window).

claims.text: Look for: free fluid in the pouch of Douglas (rectouterine, F) or rectovesical pouch (M). In females also look for IUP vs ectopic when pregnancy + trauma
claims.quote: Free fluid in pouch of Douglas (rectouterine, F) or rectovesical pouch (M). In females also evaluate for IUP vs ectopic in setting of pregnancy + trauma.

claims.text: Pitfalls: empty bladder = poor view (consider clamping a Foley). Small amounts of pelvic free fluid are normal in reproductive-age females (physiologic). Bowel gas can mimic or obscure
claims.quote: Empty bladder = poor view; consider clamping Foley if needed. Pelvic free fluid is normal in small amounts in reproductive-age females (physiologic). Bowel gas can mimic or obscure.

claims.text: eFAST anterior chest view (pneumothorax) Probe: linear probe, midclavicular line at the 2nd-4th intercostal spaces on both sides, indicator cephalad. Find the pleural line between two ribs (“bat sign”)
claims.quote: Linear probe, midclavicular line at 2nd-4th intercostal spaces bilaterally, indicator cephalad. Identify pleural line between two ribs ('bat sign').

claims.text: Look for: lung sliding (pleural line shimmers with respiration) = NO pneumothorax. Absent sliding + “barcode/stratosphere sign” on M-mode = pneumothorax. Lung point (transition between sliding and non-sliding) is pathognomonic
claims.quote: Lung sliding (pleural line shimmers with respiration) = NO pneumothorax. Absent sliding + 'barcode/stratosphere sign' on M-mode = pneumothorax. Lung point (transition between sliding and non-sliding) is pathognomonic.

claims.text: Pitfalls: bullae, pleural adhesions, mainstem intubation and prior pleurodesis → false absent sliding. Confirm with upright CXR or CT if equivocal
claims.quote: Bullae, pleural adhesions, mainstem intubation, prior pleurodesis → false absent sliding. Sensitivity ~88-90%, specificity ~99%. Confirm with upright CXR or CT if equivocal.
